turns.doctor_question: Hello. I'm Dr. Smith. To get us started, could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response: Hi, Dr. Smith. Um, well, I guess the main thing is I just can't seem to stay on track with anything. Like, I'll be sitting down, trying to fill out a job application—which I really need to do because I've been out of work for a bit, and my buddy was telling me about this warehouse gig, but honestly, I don't even know if I want to do warehouse work again. I did it a couple years ago after high school, and the manager was this guy who always breathed out of his mouth, it was so weird. But anyway, yeah, I'll be trying to work on the application, and then a car will drive by outside, or my phone buzzes, or I just think of some random idea, and suddenly I'm doing something completely different. I don't even notice it happening until an hour later and the application is still blank.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient reports an inability to stay on track with tasks, such as sitting down to fill out a job application and leaving it blank an hour later.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient explicitly describes being easily distracted from tasks by extraneous stimuli (a car driving by, a phone buzzing) and unrelated thoughts (random ideas).

turns.doctor_question: Looking back at your childhood, did you struggle with these same issues of being easily distracted or having trouble staying on task in school or at home?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, yeah, for sure. Even way back in elementary school, it was a whole thing. My teachers were constantly moving my seat. Like, I'd come in on a Monday and my name tag would be in a totally different spot. I remember in fourth grade, Mr. Henderson—he had this crazy comb-over that would literally flap up when the AC kicked on—he moved me right next to the class pet. It was this bearded dragon named Spike. Spike just sat under a heat lamp and ate crickets all day, which is honestly kind of a boring life if you think about it. I don't know why people keep lizards, they don't even play with you. 

But anyway, Mr. Henderson moved me over there because I was always talking out of turn and just blurting stuff out during lessons. And I’d always forget my homework. Or I'd actually try to do it, but I’d just rush through the worksheets so fast so I could go outside, and they'd just be full of all these careless mistakes. And then I'd lose the paper in my backpack anyway. My backpack was basically a black hole back then. I once found a crushed juice box in there from like three months prior that had leaked over everything... wait, what was the question again? Oh, right, school. But yeah, I guess I've always kind of been like this.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient states they would rush through worksheets and make careless mistakes.
symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient explicitly agrees ('Oh, yeah, for sure') to the doctor's question about having trouble staying on task.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient mentions they would always forget their homework.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient describes their backpack as a 'black hole', indicating severe difficulty with organization.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient notes they would frequently lose their papers in their backpack.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient confirms the doctor's question about being easily distracted and demonstrates it mid-response by going on a tangent and forgetting the question.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient admits to 'blurting stuff out during lessons' and talking out of turn.

turns.doctor_question: When you think back to your time in school, would you say that you were more often physically restless—like having trouble staying in your seat or needing to move around—or was your primary struggle mostly just staying focused on the task at hand?
turns.patient_response:
Man, I don't even know if I could pick one over the other. It felt like both? I definitely couldn't sit still, but to be fair, those chairs we had in school were the absolute worst. You know those hard plastic ones with the metal legs? Our school put cut-up tennis balls on the bottom of all of them so they wouldn't scratch the linoleum floor. 

I always wondered who had to sit there and cut thousands of tennis balls. Like, did the janitor just spend his whole summer doing that? Or did they buy them pre-cut? Anyway, I used to reach down and pick the yellow fuzz off them while the teacher was talking. Actually, one time in seventh grade I picked a tennis ball completely bald, just down to the bare rubber. My math teacher, Mrs. Gable, got so mad at me. She was also the gym teacher, which is kind of a weird combo if you think about it. Usually the gym teachers just teach health, not pre-algebra. But she was super intense. We used to play dodgeball in her class until the district banned it because this kid Tyler took a ball right to the nose and bled all over the gym floor. It was a whole big drama, his mom came in and yelled at the principal and everything. 

But um... wait, what did you ask me? Something about staying in my seat?

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient agrees ('It felt like both?') that they struggled with staying focused on tasks in school.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient gets highly distracted by unrelated thoughts about chairs, janitors, and dodgeball, ultimately forgetting the doctor's question.
symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient describes fidgeting in class by picking the yellow fuzz off the tennis balls on the chair legs.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly states, 'I definitely couldn't sit still,' confirming physical restlessness.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient provides a long, rambling, and tangential monologue, demonstrating excessive talking.

turns.doctor_question: Do you feel like you are still constantly moving or physically restless in situations where you are expected to stay seated, like in a movie theater or at a work desk?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, definitely. I mean, I can't really sit still anywhere, especially now. See, I used to play soccer a lot, like, in a men's league on Thursday nights. It was pretty competitive, actually. Our team was called the Grass Kickers, which I thought was hilarious, but my buddy Steve came up with it and he's not even that funny usually. He works in accounting and wears these really weird ties with, like, Looney Tunes characters on them. Who wears a Tazmanian Devil tie in 2023, you know? 

But anyway, I messed up my knee a while back playing pickup basketball—which is ironic because I'm not even good at basketball—so I haven't been able to play soccer. And since I can't play like I used to, just sitting around the house is brutal. It literally makes me feel like I'm crawling out of my skin. I just end up pacing from room to room, looking out the windows, checking the fridge even though I know there's nothing in there but half a jar of pickles and some old mustard. I really need to go to the grocery store, actually. But yeah, sitting at a desk or in a theater? Forget about it. I feel like my legs have their own heartbeat.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates distractibility by frequently interrupting his own answer with unrelated thoughts about his friend's tie and needing to go to the grocery store.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient indicates an inability to remain seated in expected situations, noting that sitting at a desk or in a theater is impossible and that he ends up pacing from room to room.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly confirms severe physical restlessness, describing the sensation as 'crawling out of my skin' and feeling like his 'legs have their own heartbeat'.

turns.doctor_question: Do you find that you often act without thinking, such as blurting out answers or interrupting others in conversation, even when you know you shouldn't?
turns.patient_response: Oh, yeah, for sure. I cut people off a lot. It's like an answer just pops into my head and I have to say it right then, before they're even done talking. I do it to my mom all the time. She gets so annoyed with me. And my counselor too, I'm always interrupting him. He's this really quiet guy, wears these round glasses that make him look like Harry Potter, but older. He's got this weird habit of tapping his pen on his knee when he's listening. Click, click, click. It's a silver pen, looks expensive, maybe a Parker or something? I used to have a nice pen once, someone gave it to me for graduation, but I lost it like three days later. Left it at a coffee shop, I think. Or maybe it fell out of my pocket on the bus. I used to take the 42 bus all the time, the one that goes past the old mall that's mostly empty now. They have this one pretzel place left in there that's actually really good, but everything else is boarded up. It's kind of sad, honestly, just walking through there and seeing all those closed stores. You know, they used to have a huge arcade there when I was a kid... wait, what were we talking about? Interrupting? Right, yeah, I definitely do that. I just blurt things out before I can stop myself.

symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient mentions losing a nice pen shortly after receiving it.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient gets distracted by unrelated thoughts (the counselor's pen, losing a pen, the bus, the mall) and loses track of the conversation.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly states they blurt things out and say answers before others are done talking.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient confirms they frequently cut people off and interrupt others, such as their mom and counselor.
